title: The Newspaper Editorial Is Disappearing
hook: Pulitzer editorial entries fell from 101 in 1995 to 25 this year, as chains swapped local editorials for syndicated columns — leaving a hole in local accountability.
key_points: Pulitzer Prize editorial-category entries dropped from 101 (1995) to 25 this year; the Pulitzer board folded editorials into a broader opinion category.
Since 2022, Gannett and Lee Enterprises — the two largest U.S. newspaper chains — replaced many local editorials with standardized, syndicated national opinion pages.
Gannett said editorials were 'frequently cited' by readers as a reason for canceling subscriptions.
The author proposes three fixes: publish editorials only when they truly matter, build community editorial boards of local civic voices, and pool candidate-interview reporting across outlets.
content_html: American newspaper editorials have shrunk dramatically as a civic institution. Pulitzer Prize entries in the editorial category fell from 101 in 1995 to just 25 this year — a decline so steep the Pulitzer board eventually folded editorials into a broader opinion category. Since 2022, Gannett and Lee Enterprises, the two largest U.S. newspaper chains, have replaced many local editorials with standardized, syndicated national opinion pages, even though Gannett itself found editorials were "frequently cited" by readers as a reason for canceling subscriptions.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, longtime editor Ken Paulson traces the editorial's history back to Horace Greeley's standalone editorial page in 1841 — a tradition that helped drive abolitionism, women's suffrage, and challenges to wartime civil-liberties abuses. His concern is that as editorials vanish, so does one channel through which local news held officials accountable. He proposes three concrete fixes: publish editorials more selectively so each one carries real weight; build community editorial boards drawing on diverse local civic voices rather than a single staff writer; and have outlets pool candidate-interview and endorsement reporting so smaller newsrooms can sustain the practice at lower cost.

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Ken Paulson, Director of the Free Speech Center, Middle Tennessee State University
